sections.html:
Alabama's largest county by population is Jefferson, hub of the Birmingham-Hoover metro area, home to 665,742 people by the 2025 estimate. Birmingham is the seat. Its cities range from Bessemer and Hoover to Homewood, Vestavia Hills, Mountain Brook, Trussville and Gardendale, with Hueytown, Pleasant Grove, Center Point and Fultondale among the others, and many small communities sit outside any city.

Mining and steelmaking shaped the map. Many neighborhoods started as company towns, and Ensley, North Birmingham, Woodlawn and Elyton were absorbed into Birmingham. Housing in those areas skews old, and family-held homes there often sell after a death rather than through a normal listing.

Watch the county lines. Birmingham, Hoover, Vestavia Hills, Helena, Leeds and Trussville each reach partly across the line, and so do Sumiton and Warrior. Whichever county holds the parcel sends the bill, regardless of the city on your envelope.

One statewide calendar governs every Alabama county, Jefferson included. Payment is expected by October 1, and nonpayment becomes delinquency when the year ends.

WhenStep in the cycle
October 1Tax due
January 1Tax delinquent
FebruaryDelinquent accounts sent to probate court
MarchProbate court meets
AprilParcels advertised for sale
MayTax sale

Each bill pays for the tax year that finished the previous September 30, so a fall payment looks backward. A sale in the middle of the year means the closer divides that year's tax between seller and buyer.

Three classes apply. Class I, utilities, is assessed at 30 percent. Class II, a catch-all for other property, is 20 percent. Class III is 10 percent and covers farmland, timber and a single-family home where the owner lives.

Appraised value times the class rate yields assessed value, and exemptions come off that figure. A home you live in gets the 10 percent rate, while a rental or second home may be assessed higher than the primary residence next door. Landlords selling a Jefferson County rental are sometimes surprised by this.

You usually must apply for an exemption, and amounts differ from one county to the next. Ask Jefferson County what fits your situation rather than trusting a figure from another county.

Most questions land at one of two desks. Values and appeals belong to the tax assessor. Bills and payments belong to the tax collector. Should a bill never come, call the collector: the state does not make the county get one to you in advance, so the duty stays with you.

The probate court is its own office. It records your deed once a house sells, and delinquent accounts pass into its hands under the state schedule. Rates are fixed through the statutory process, not by local home rule, and Jefferson County has no calendar of its own.

On any call, keep the parcel number handy and say whether your question concerns value, a bill or a payoff. Each question belongs to a different desk, and starting at the right one saves a transfer and a second call.

The first notice after a sale may still name the previous owner. Under state practice the notice stays with whoever was on record the prior October 1, together with that owner's exemptions. Liability goes with the property, though, so the current owner owes the tax whatever the paper says.

At the closing table, sellers should check three things:

  • This year's tax has been paid or divided.
  • Earlier delinquent tax comes out of the proceeds.
  • You keep the payoff statement.

For a purchase made before October 1, the buyer has until December 31 to record the deed, get the property assessed in their name and claim exemptions.

An unpaid account keeps traveling toward the May sale, picking up penalties, interest and advertising costs each month. The balance only grows.

Selling before the auction is usually simpler, because the title company can deduct the tax from your proceeds. Should the debt exceed what the house would net, tell the title company the numbers at the outset.

Get a written payoff from the collector and pass it to the closer. Lenders will not fund while the lien stands, and cash buyers want the same figure on the settlement sheet.

sections.h2: Where Jefferson County sellers get stuck
sections.html:
• Estate sales in older Birmingham neighborhoods with several heirs.
  • Rental houses with a higher tax class and deferred repairs.
  • Houses whose delinquent tax is heading for the spring sale.
  • Parcels near a county line where the billing office is not obvious.
  • Out-of-state owners who have never seen a bill.

Owners living elsewhere can start with the parcel number and ask the collector where bills have been going. With an estate, work out who holds title before anyone signs a contract, since the deed must be in order for a closing to happen.

Cash Home Buyers makes written offers on Jefferson County houses in their current condition. A local title company runs the closing and pays unpaid tax from the sale proceeds. Because no lender is involved, there is no appraisal to wait on and no repair list to negotiate.

sections.h2: How a cash sale works from offer to closing
sections.html:
The steps are short. You describe the house and the parcel, a written offer follows, and you choose the closing date. A local title company then searches the record for liens, including any tax that is owed, and prepares the settlement statement.

Because tax is settled at the closing table, an old balance does not have to be paid in advance out of your own pocket. The title company subtracts it from the sale price and sends the rest to you. If the search turns up a surprise, such as a missing heir on a deed, you hear about it early and can fix it before the closing date instead of on the day.

sections.h2: What to gather before you list
sections.html:
A small folder helps. Pull your latest tax notice or receipt, the parcel number, the recorded deed and any exemption paperwork you filed. After a death, add the documents showing who holds title now.

Next, phone the tax collector and ask whether anything is owed for this year or earlier. If your address is in a city that crosses a county line, ask which county bills the parcel. Armed with those answers, a title company can estimate what you would net without guessing.

Write down the names and dates of every call. If a figure later turns out different, you will have a record of who quoted it.

Also ask your mortgage servicer whether the lender pays the tax from escrow. If it does, the servicer's records will show what was paid and when, which makes the closing math easier.

faqs.q: When is Jefferson County property tax due?
faqs.a: October 1 is the due date. The account becomes delinquent after December 31.

faqs.q: What is the Alabama property tax timetable?
faqs.a: Delinquency starts January 1. Accounts go to probate court in February, the court meets in March, parcels are advertised in April, and the sale takes place in May.

faqs.q: What property classes does Alabama use?
faqs.a: Utilities are Class I at 30 percent. Everything else is Class II at 20 percent. Class III covers agricultural land, timber and owner-occupied single-family homes at 10 percent.

faqs.q: Why is my Jefferson County tax bill in the previous owner's name?
faqs.a: The notice stays under the name on record the previous October 1. You still owe the tax as the new owner, so check that it has been paid.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Jefferson County house with unpaid property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. The title company gets a payoff figure from the tax office and pays it from your proceeds at closing. If your city crosses a county line, the county where the parcel sits is the one that bills.
